title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
summary:
The Windows Command Shell, implemented by cmd.exe, is the legacy interpreter for batch files and interactive command execution on Windows. It provides built-in commands for file manipulation, process and service control, network configuration, and scheduled task creation, and it acts as a launcher for other utilities. Adversaries favour it because it is universally present, is not typically removed by hardening, and blends with a very high volume of legitimate administrative and installer traffic. Typical abuse patterns involve chaining built-in commands together with shell redirection and the command separator to perform discovery, staging, and cleanup within a single short-lived process.

The artefacts left behind are concentrated in process creation telemetry. The parent process is often more informative than cmd.exe itself, because the shell is frequently spawned by a document reader, a script host, a service, or a webshell. Command lines containing long chains of separators, repeated directory traversal toward temporary or public directories, and redirection into executable file types are notable. Script Block Logging does not cover cmd.exe, so visibility depends on command line auditing, the process creation event source used by the endpoint agent, and file and registry events generated by whatever the shell touched. Batch files executed from user-writable paths leave a file creation record that may be deleted immediately afterwards.

Routine use includes login scripts, software deployment wrappers, backup jobs, and diagnostic commands run by administrators. The distinguishing factors are context and sequence: an unusual parent, a service account running console utilities interactively, network share access immediately preceding shell execution, and command content that maps to discovery or staging rather than to a scheduled maintenance task. Comparing the observed command line against the standard image of the host and against known automation accounts resolves most apparent positives.
objectives: Describe how cmd.exe parses command separators, redirection, and quoting, and why that parsing shapes what appears in log records.
Extract and interpret parent-child process relationships that indicate a shell spawned by an unexpected host application.
Build SIEM-style queries that surface anomalous command shell usage while suppressing known installer and login script noise.
Reconstruct a short shell session from command line auditing, file creation, and registry events when no script logging is available.
Explain the visibility limitations of resource kit tooling historically used to log console activity and how it fails on modern systems.
Map observed shell behaviour to ATT&CK and document the specific telemetry gaps that remain in the environment.
